passage_parts.label: A
passage_parts.title: Text A: A Blacksmith Remembers
passage_parts.text:
I started bending iron in a small workshop when I was still a teenager. In those days, almost every new house in town wanted iron grilles on its windows. Families were finally earning enough to build homes of their own, and the grilles kept thieves out of the ground floor and stopped children from falling out of the rooms upstairs. But nobody wanted plain bars. Customers asked for a vase, which stood for peace, or a dragon and a phoenix for good luck, and some even had their family name worked into the design. My boss charged by weight, so a rich pattern cost more, and he hung our finest pieces outside the shop to attract new business.
Then the work slowly dried up. Stainless steel and aluminum frames never rusted and could be turned out by machines, while our black iron had to be scraped and repainted again and again. Nowadays, when an old house is torn down, its grilles usually end up as scrap metal. Sometimes I walk past a building site and recognize my own work lying in the pile.

passage_parts.label: B
passage_parts.title: Text B: Old Patterns, New Homes
passage_parts.text: Designer Chen Yi-hsuan runs a small studio that gives the patterns of old iron grilles a second life. To her, the grilles are like the faces of old houses. “Each family chose its own design, so a grille tells you who lived behind it and what they hoped for,” she says. “Every time one is thrown away, a piece of that story disappears.” Whenever she can, Chen reuses the old iron itself. If a grille is too rusty to go back on a window, she keeps a single flower or cloud from it and builds a lamp or a plant pot around it. Other patterns she copies by hand onto key rings and room dividers. Is the craft dying? Chen does not think so. “The skills are still here; what has disappeared is demand,” she explains. Hand-made grilles are now priced by the days of work rather than by weight, so few families order them for their windows anymore. “Small objects won’t change that overnight,” she admits, “but they quietly bring the old patterns back into people’s homes.”

translation_zh.text:
【文本 A：一位鐵匠的回憶】
我還是個青少年的時候，就在一間小工坊裡開始彎鐵。那時候，鎮上幾乎每一棟新房子都想在窗戶裝上鐵窗。家家戶戶終於賺夠了錢，能蓋自己的房子；鐵窗能把小偷擋在一樓外面，也能防止孩子從樓上的房間摔出去。可是沒有人想要光禿禿的鐵條。客人會要一個花瓶，代表平安，或是一龍一鳳，象徵好運，有些人甚至把自家的姓氏做進圖案裡。老闆按重量收費，所以花樣越繁複就越貴；他還把我們最精美的作品掛在店門外招攬新生意。
後來，工作慢慢變少了。不鏽鋼和鋁做的窗框從不生鏽，又能用機器大量生產；而我們的黑鐵得一再刮除、重新上漆。現在，老房子一拆，鐵窗花通常就成了廢鐵。有時候我經過工地，會在廢料堆裡認出自己的作品。

【文本 B：老圖案，新的家】
設計師陳宜萱經營一間小工作室，讓老鐵窗花的圖案獲得第二次生命。對她來說，鐵窗花就像老房子的臉。「每個家庭都選了自己的圖案，所以一扇鐵窗花會告訴你，是誰住在它後面、他們懷抱著什麼希望，」她說。「每丟掉一扇，那段故事就少了一塊。」
只要可以，陳宜萱就會重新利用舊的鐵件本身。如果一扇鐵窗花鏽得太厲害、裝不回窗上，她會從中留下一朵花或一朵雲，再以它為中心做成一盞燈或一個盆栽。其他圖案則由她親手複製到鑰匙圈和屏風上。
這門手藝正在消失嗎？陳宜萱不這麼認為。「技術都還在；消失的是需求，」她解釋。手工鐵窗花現在是按工作天數、而不是按重量計價，所以很少家庭再訂來裝在窗戶上。「小東西沒辦法一夜之間改變這件事，」她承認，「但它們能悄悄把老圖案帶回人們的家裡。」
